title: Injury Q&A #3
summary: NH answers viewer injury questions: brachialis-area pain when pressing, forearm splints, an uneven chest, hip flexor tightness and squat hip pain, sternum popping on dips, a distal biceps rupture on incline curls, nagging hamstrings on wide-stance work, and an elbow nerve that snaps on pressing. His recurring themes are stacked joints, finger-extension work, avoiding movements your structure dislikes, and building muscle around vulnerable joints.
claims: Injury prevention matters most: if you're injured you can't train and can't grow, so always accumulate tonnage safely
Pain where forearm meets biceps when pressing is less dangerous than distal biceps tendon pain because it is muscle tension, not a tendon that can snap
Forearm angle matters on the bench; keeping the forearm fully stacked and straight prevents pain, while internal or external rotation creates a weak link
Add 2-3 sets of forearm isolation at the end of the day to see if it helps forearm pain
Train finger and hand extension with rubber band finger extenders; it relieves forearm, elbow, shoulder and neck pain and builds bigger forearms
Use a medicine ball pressed into the crook of the elbow or rolled along the forearm to release tension
Forearms are among the most constantly tense muscles and tend to calcify; the same happens to traps of stressed people
Use straps to rest the grip; they also give the forearms a bigger stretch since you hold more weight
Contrast showers on the forearms after training, alternating hot and cold, increase blood flow for recovery
An uneven chest usually comes from one shoulder sitting higher, so the other side travels through more range of motion and grows more
Fix an uneven chest by correcting bar path, adding isometric band squeezes for the lagging side, and 2-3 extra one-arm dumbbell bench sets per chest day
Better leverage means a muscle has to work less, so the smaller side may actually be stronger because of better positioning
Long sitting tightens hip flexors, which can lead to back problems; stretch them after every leg day
Hip flexor stretch: seated, cross one leg over the other and press on the knee, cautiously, because cold, short hip flexors can tear
He used to have very bad hip flexor pain and fixed it with stretches; it never came back
Hip pain in squats often means tight hip flexors; lower the weight or cut range of motion slightly until they are lengthened
Once hip flexors are lengthened, little work is needed to maintain them
Joint noises rank low among warning signs; pain or a feeling that something shifted matters more
Sternum cracking on dips without pain is fine, possibly cartilage or rib cage expansion; avoid big dip PRs and going beyond your range
Incline dumbbell curls tempt people to overextend past a useful range, lock the elbow and bounce off the tendon, which does nothing for hypertrophy and causes injuries like distal biceps ruptures
Full range of motion is not always the best range; the best range targets the muscle, and for biceps the elbow must stay slightly flexed
Locking out on triceps extensions repeatedly can cause tennis elbow; proper curls that strengthen the antagonist help prevent it
Some bodies dislike certain movement patterns; he cannot squat or pull wide stance because of narrow hips and a large waist
For hamstring pain at the hip in wide-stance squats, deadlifts, Bulgarian split squats and lunges, drop those movements; legs can be trained other ways
Use active stretches like Romanian deadlifts, hyperextensions and glute ham raises to lengthen the hamstrings and glutes
Long-standing pain that never snapped is likely structural and under control, not a freak injury waiting to happen
People who can't do any movement pattern at all don't exist, but some can't do certain categories of movements
The overhead press past eye level becomes a mostly triceps and elbow-driven press, which is why triceps often limit it
If overhead pressing hurts the elbow, try incline presses, pike or handstand push-ups which involve more shoulder flexion
Build the triceps heads with extensions to create a muscle cushion around a vulnerable elbow; muscles protect tendons
Building the rear delts and traps brings unstable or dislocating shoulders under control
exercises: open the fingers against a rubber band
trains neglected hand extension, relieves forearm pain
2-3 extra sets for the lagging side
squeeze hard at the top, isometric
cross leg over, press on knee slowly
injury risk to the distal biceps tendon
more shoulder, less triceps; elbow-friendly alternative to OHP
builds long head, cushions the elbow
